report:
## Conclusion: The evidence does **not** support that saw palmetto improves BPH symptoms long-term versus placebo.

Your sister's conviction is not supported by the best available evidence. Here is what the key studies show:

**The STEP Trial (NEJM, 2006):** The most influential long-term study randomized 225 men with moderate-to-severe BPH to saw palmetto extract (160 mg twice daily) or placebo for **one full year**. The result: saw palmetto was **not superior to placebo** for improving urinary symptoms or objective measures of BPH. (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa053085)

**The CAMUS Trial (JAMA, 2011):** Researchers tested even **escalating doses** of saw palmetto (up to 960 mg/day, three times the standard dose) versus placebo over 72 weeks. Again, saw palmetto **failed to outperform placebo** on symptom scores or urinary flow measures. (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/1104439)

**Cochrane Systematic Review (2020):** The updated Cochrane review concluded that *Serenoa repens* (saw palmetto) monotherapy provides **"little to no benefit"** for men with lower urinary tract symptoms due to BPH. (https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD004407.pub4/full)

**NCCIH (2023):** The U.S. National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health reviewed 27 studies and concluded that saw palmetto, when used alone, provides **"little or no benefit"** for BPH symptoms. (https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/saw-palmetto)

**Bottom line:** While some older, smaller, lower-quality trials suggested modest benefits, the largest, most rigorous, placebo-controlled trials and the most recent systematic reviews consistently show that saw palmetto does **not** meaningfully improve BPH symptoms beyond placebo in the longer term. Your sister's answer of "yes" is not supported by current evidence.
